paras: The reported expulsion of Black residents from Eldorado, Illinois, is known only from a remark by Senator Tillman that the people of the town had "recently chased every negro out of the town," printed in a Washington dispatch of February 26, 1903. Tillman offered it as evidence that white northerners were as hostile to Black people as white southerners, and no other report of the episode was found.

The remark came while southern senators were discussing a report from Indiana, Pennsylvania, that "the whole negro population of the town had been driven out because of a crime of one negro." Speaking of that case, Tillman said it illustrated his recent speech and that Black migration north was "teaching a very practical lesson to the northern white man."

After claiming he could name at least eight towns in Indiana that would not let a Black newcomer "land," Tillman added that the people of Eldorado had recently chased every Black resident out. He gave no date, cause, number of people affected or account of how they were driven out, and named no one involved. No local or wire report describing an expulsion at Eldorado appears in the coverage, and no arrests or official response were reported.

The Birmingham Age-Herald printed the Washington special on February 27 under the headline "Negroes Are Driven Out of Pennsylvania Town," with the Eldorado sentence buried in the continuation of Tillman's comments. The paper reported his words without comment on either expulsion.

A different version of the same remarks, dated February 27 and printed by the Keowee Courier of South Carolina on March 11 under "Want No Negroes North," called Tillman's speech "magnificent" and put the Pennsylvania "outrage" in quotation marks. That version kept his point about the Indiana towns but did not mention Eldorado. No Black-press coverage of an expulsion at Eldorado was found.

reader.title: Reported expulsion of Black residents from Eldorado, Illinois
bases: The only report says the people of Eldorado 'chased every negro out of the town,' a removal of the whole Black population, not an attack on named persons (A2).

The event rests on one sentence attributed to Senator Tillman in a single Washington special (A1, A2); no local, wire or Black-press report of it was found, and another version of the same remarks omits it (A3).
